title: Xbox satılık mı? CEO Asha Sharma iddialara yanıt verdi
summary: Xbox CEO'su Asha Sharma, şirketin satışta olduğu yönündeki iddiaları yalanlayarak, markayı başarıya ulaştırmak için ne gerekiyorsa yapacaklarını belirtti.
body:
Xbox satılık mı sorusu, son dönemde yaşanan büyük çaplı işten çıkarmalar ve stüdyo değişikliklerinin ardından gündeme gelmeye devam ederken, şirketten net bir açıklama geldi. Xbox CEO'su Asha Sharma, The New York Times'a yaptığı açıklamada, markanın kesinlikle satışta olmadığını vurguladı.

## Kapsamlı yeniden yapılandırma ve stüdyo değişiklikleri

Bu yıl içinde bir kurumsal "reset" sürecine giren Xbox, gelecek yaza kadar toplamda 3.200 çalışanın işine son vermeyi planlıyor. Bu süreçte Double Fine, Compulsion Games ve Undead Labs bağımsız stüdyolar haline gelirken; Halo serisinin yönetimi Activision'a devredildi. Rare, World's Edge ve Obsidian Entertainment gibi isimler de farklı çatı altında yeniden konumlandırıldı. Sektör analistleri bu adımların şirketi olası bir alıcı için daha cazip hale getirmeyi amaçladığını öne sürerken, eski PlayStation yöneticisi Shawn Laydon ise mevcut durumu Sega'nın geçmişteki donanım pazarından çekilişine benzeterek Xbox yönetimine "bir yol seçin" tavsiyesinde bulundu.

## Asha Sharma'dan net duruş

Tüm bu tartışmalara ve kulislerde konuşulan ihtimallere rağmen CEO Asha Sharma, Microsoft ile uzun vadeli bir yolda olduklarını ifade etti. Sharma, The New York Times'a verdiği demeçte, "Xbox satılık değil… Şirketi başarıya ulaştırmak için ne gerekiyorsa yapacağız ve doğru ortaklıkları, doğru iş modelini ve bunu başarmak için gereken her şeyi değerlendireceğiz" dedi.

**Neden önemli?** Xbox'ın yaşadığı büyük yapısal dönüşüm ve artan maliyetler oyun sektöründe geleceğe dair soru işaretleri yaratırken, yönetim tarafındaki kararlı duruş markanın donanım ve yazılım stratejilerinde uzun vadeli planlarına devam edeceğini gösteriyor.

source_texts.title: "Xbox is not for sale": CEO Asha Sharma says "we will do whatever it takes" to turn the console maker's fortunes around
source_texts.summary: Despite mass layoffs at multiple first-party studios and major internal shakeups, CEO Asha Sharma has shot down speculation about a potential Xbox buyout. Read more
source_texts.text:
Despite mass layoffs at multiple first-party studios and major internal shakeups, CEO Asha Sharma has shot down speculation about a potential Xbox buyout.
This year, Xbox began a corporate "reset" that plans to cut a total of 3,200 jobs across the company before next summer. So far, the restructure has resulted in three studios going independent (Double Fine, Compulsion Games, Undead Labs), while the fate of Hellblade maker Ninja Theory and Dishonored studio Arkane remains up in the air.
In another dramatic turn earlier this month, Xbox handed Activision the keys to the entire Halo series. Rare and World's Edge (of Age of Empires fame) also moved under the Call of Duty publisher, while Obsidian Entertainment got slotted into Bethesda. That leaves only a handful of developers under the Xbox Game Studios umbrella - The Coalition (Gears of War), Playground Games (Fable, Forza), Mojang (Minecraft), InXile Entertainment (Clockwork Revolution) and what's left of Halo Studios.
To many, this looked like an attempt at streamlining the business to make it more attractive for potential buyers. (Microsoft might have struggled to sell Rare by itself, for example, but that becomes a much easier task when it's bundled in with the company in control of Call of Duty.) A sale isn't on the table at all, however, according to Sharma.
Speaking to The New York Times, she put it plainly: "Xbox is not for sale… We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that."
As NYT noted, Sharma's answer doesn't completely rule out the possibility of Xbox being spun off as an independent entity that still works closely with Microsoft, like some analysts have suggested. There's no signs of that so far, at least.
"We've got a long way to go with Microsoft," Sharma added, “and we're going to take the long-term view."
From here, the console maker is hoping next week's Gears of War: E-Day and next year's Clockwork Revolution can still make a splash as Xbox console exclusives. Sharma also recently signed a deal with Kojima Productions on its action-stealth game Physint, after rival PlayStation pulled funding from the project.

source_texts.title: 'This Is Your Dreamcast Moment' — Former PlayStation Boss Offers New Xbox CEO Some Words of Advice
source_texts.summary: Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden has offered new Xbox CEO some words of advice as she resets Microsoft’s gaming business: “pick a lane.”
source_texts.text:
Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden has offered new Xbox CEO some words of advice as she resets Microsoft’s gaming business: “pick a lane.”
In an interview with The Expansion Pass, the former boss of Sony Interactive Entertainment America called the decision Asha Sharma now faces Xbox’s “Dreamcast moment.”
This is a reference to Sega’s earth-shattering exit from the console business following the commercial failure of the Dreamcast. That call, made early 2001, ended a run of console manufacturing that included the likes of the Sega Genesis, Game Gear, and Sega Saturn. Sega instead focused on releasing video games on previously rival consoles, such as Sony's PS2.
Fast forward 25 years, and Xbox is in the middle of a dramatic restructure that has already seen nearly 2,000 staff lose their jobs, multiple studios either exit Xbox or face closure, and various games canceled. Xbox is now focused on fewer, bigger video game franchises such as The Elder Scrolls, Fallout, and Minecraft, with the likes of Halo moved over to Call of Duty company Activision. Through it all, there are question marks hanging over the viability of Xbox’s confirmed next-gen console, Project Helix.
With this in mind, Layden was asked if he had any advice for Sharma, having led a video game business of his own. He presented two options: go hard on taking on PlayStation now and in the future, with the assumed launch of Project Helix and PlayStation 6, or pack up those console plans and focus on software.
“You got to pick a lane,” he began. “Either you're going to be a platform competitive with PlayStation — which Xbox has not been competitive with PlayStation for years — but that's not out of the window. You know, you can still make another run at it. And there are certain decisions you have to make around that about the platform. We talked about exclusivity. We talked about, how do you incentivize third-parties to support your platform in a meaningful way? This is all things around the platform business.
“Or you sit back and realize you are the biggest game publisher in the world. Well maybe Tencent’s bigger, but in the Western world you are the biggest game publisher out there with Activision and Blizzard and Bethesda and all the other pieces. Be that. This is your Dreamcast moment, when Sega decided we're just going to be on PS2 and we're going to get out of the hardware business and just be a great software company. It can be done. It's been done before. So, that's my advice. Pick a lane.”

Microsoft has for years now fended off questions over whether it plans to exit the console hardware business amid poor sales of Xbox Series X and S and, before it, Xbox One. Publicly, Microsoft boss Satya Nadella and Asha Sharma have remained committed to console hardware, with Sharma saying it’s central to the company’s gaming plans. But Sharma has also said in recent months that Microsoft needs to think carefully about how Xbox consoles work and make money, particularly with the RAMpocalypse driving up prices.
In June, Sharma said the spiralling cost of new and existing consoles would require "radically different business models" over the coming generation. Speaking to Fortune, Sharma acknowledged the increasing price of existing hardware and components — fuelled by global crises and the rise of AI — and said the industry had "reached a point where it will be hard to imagine" mass audiences still being able to afford "thousands of dollars" for a new console generation.
And just this week, former PlayStation executive Shuhei Yoshida said Sony and Nintendo needed to make their current consoles last as long as possible amid soaring costs that have already prompted PS5 and Switch 2 price rises.
Big questions remain. What, exactly, does Project Helix look like? How far down the exclusivity road will Xbox go? And here’s the biggest of all: will Xbox eventually exit the console business?
